subsections.title: Random 6 mode
subsections.html:
Random 6 pulls a short six-problem sample out of a quiz set’s problem bank, a quick way to check where you stand without committing to the whole set. Every problem is picked fresh each time you start one, so back-to-back attempts rarely look the same.

There are two ways to draw that sample:

Single draws all 6 problems from just the quiz set you have selected. Cumulative widens the pool to every quiz set you’ve unlocked so far, so once you’re working through quiz set 3, a cumulative Random 6 can also hand you a problem from sets 1 or 2, which is closer to what a cumulative final actually feels like. In cumulative mode you can also narrow that pool with filters (more on that just below).

Filters live in the Problem Pool Filter panel and only apply in cumulative mode: pick specific quiz sets, a topic, or a range of problem numbers to draw from instead of the full unlocked pool. A small notice above the quiz reminds you a filter is active while it’s on, and Reset filter preferences clears it back to drawing from everything.

Random 6 is also the only mode that times you. Once you check your answers, that attempt’s score and per-problem breakdown are saved into your stats panel automatically. Solve Them All is meant for unhurried, full-bank practice instead, so it doesn’t carry a timer or log individual attempts there.

One of the things Random 6 (and every other mode) leans on is that most problems aren’t just text: a lot of them ship with a dynamic figure, redrawn by hand as vector illustrations rather than pasted-in screenshots. Because they’re real vector shapes built from theme variables instead of static images, they automatically restyle with whatever color theme and light/dark mode you’re using elsewhere in the app. Here’s the actual illustration from quiz set 2, problem 36, dropped in as a live demo. Try the day/night toggle and the little color dots below it:

Demonstration of quiz 2 problem 36 adaptive illustration.

subsections.title: Solve them all mode
subsections.html:
Solve Them All runs the entire problem bank for a quiz set back to back, instead of a random sample, with every problem laid out as its own card that you work through at your own pace. It respects the same single/cumulative setting as Random 6, so a cumulative Solve Them All run pulls in every set you’ve unlocked, not just the one currently selected.

Each card is checked independently: get it right and the card locks in as correct; get it wrong, or right value but wrong unit, and it stays open for another attempt rather than moving on for you. A See correct answer button appears once you’ve gotten something wrong, in case you’d rather look it up than keep guessing; using it reveals the answer and locks that card too.

Because this mode can mean rendering $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ across the entire bank at once, every expression is pre-rendered and cached locally the first time you open it. Reopening Solve Them All later, even after closing the tab, skips that re-render entirely, so the whole set appears instantly instead of visibly typesetting in front of you. Note! Sometimes due to cache collisions, the $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ layout may become distorted with all equations displayed as a mess. Tap the "Rerender Equations" button in this case.

Your progress through a run (what’s answered, what’s locked, what you’ve typed into still-open cards) is saved automatically as you go, and syncs across your devices if you’re signed in under the same identity, so switching from your laptop to your phone picks up exactly where you left off. That per-card syncing is separate from the stats panel: Solve Them All is untimed, open-ended practice, so unlike Random 6 it doesn’t log finished attempts there.

Figures work exactly the same way here as in Random 6: every card’s illustration is a live vector shape built from theme variables, not a static image, so it restyles instantly with whatever color theme and light/dark mode you have set. Here’s that same illustration again, dropped in as a live demo:

Demonstration of quiz 2 problem 36 adaptive illustration.

subsections.title: Scoring & Answer Formatting
subsections.html:
Every answer needs a number and, where the problem calls for one, a unit. Both are checked independently.

Numeric value

Your value is checked against the stored answer with a small relative tolerance (about 1%), not an exact string match, so ordinary rounding in your working doesn’t cost you the point. Accepted number formats:

  • Plain decimals: 3.14, -0.5, 1200
  • Scientific notation with e/E: 1.6e-19, 2.998E8
  • ×10^-style notation: 5*10^3, 10^-4

A comma as a decimal separator (3,14) is not accepted: use a period.

Units

Unit boxes accept short Moodle-style unit strings: multiply units by separating them with a space (N m), divide with a slash (N/C, V/m), and raise to a power with ^ (m^2, s^-1). Real superscript characters work too: typing m² or s⁻¹ is normalized to the same thing automatically. Leaving the unit box empty is treated as dimensionless.

SI prefixes

Most base units in the course (N, C, m, s, J, V, A, T, W, H, Hz, Pa, Wb, Ohm/Ω, F) accept a standard SI prefix stuck directly on the front: type mA for milliamps or kOhm for kilohms and it’s converted automatically, relative to whatever unit the stored answer actually uses. If you can’t type μ, use u, or mc/mk as ASCII stand-ins for micro. (kg is the one exception: it already has “kilo” baked in, so stacking another prefix on it isn’t supported.)

How it's scored

Each problem is worth up to 1 point:

  • Correct (1 pt): value within tolerance and the unit matches.
  • Partial (0.9 pt): value within tolerance, but the unit is wrong or unparseable.
  • Wrong (0 pt): value outside tolerance.

subsections.title: Posting & identity
subsections.html:
You can post right away under any free-text display name, no account needed. Picking a nickname and claiming it with a 5-digit PIN turns it into a persistent identity instead: it gets its own auto-generated avatar, and you can restore that same identity on another device later by entering the nickname and PIN again. Nobody else can post under a claimed nickname without its PIN.

Start typing…
The avatars for the users are generated procedurally based on the nickname, try it out here!

A claimed identity also gets a couple of extra controls on the composer: Rename (change the nickname, same PIN and avatar carry over) and Exit this device (unlinks just this device, without touching the nickname itself or any other device it's linked to: you can always come back with the nickname and PIN).

Messages can be posted to the global thread or scoped to one specific problem, using the scope picker above the message box. Scoped messages also show up via the Discuss button on that problem itself, so a question about problem 14 stays attached to problem 14 instead of getting lost in the general thread.

You can reply directly to any message, which quotes it inline so the thread stays readable, and edit your own messages at any time after posting. There's a short pause required between posts (a few seconds) to keep the thread from being flooded.

subsections.title: Writing LaTeX in messages
subsections.html:
The forum renders $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ the same way problems do. Wrap inline math in single dollar signs, and display math (its own centered line) in double dollar signs:

The field is $E = \frac{kq}{r^2}$, pointing radially outward.

The field is $E = \frac{kq}{r^2}$, pointing radially outward.

$$\Delta V = -\int_{a}^{b} \vec{E}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{l}$$

$$\Delta V = -\int_{a}^{b} \vec{E}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{l}$$

You can also use the equation composer if you are not confident in your $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ skills yet. The $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ button next to the message box opens an equation composer with a live preview and a grid of quick-insert buttons for common things like \frac{a}{b}, \int, \sum, trig functions, and Greek letters. Click one to drop in a template, then fill in the blanks.

There's also a plain-English shorthand for when you don't want to think in $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ at all or if you are not familiar with it after all: wrap a description in single &s for inline math, or double &&s for a display equation, and it's automatically converted into real $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ before your message posts.

&E equals m c squared& becomes $E = mc^2$, and &&integral of E dot dl from a to b&& becomes a display equation the same way the hand-written example above renders. If the conversion ever fails (a connection hiccup, or something too ambiguous to interpret), you'll get the option to post your original text as-is instead of losing it.

Try it yourself

Type anything below and it’s wrapped in $$ $$ and typeset live underneath, so you can see exactly how an expression will look before posting it.

Edit the box above — the render below updates as you type.

subsections.title: Gemini, the forum bot
subsections.html:
Gemini is a bot that participates in threads when tagged. Mention @gemini anywhere in a message (typing @ opens a suggestion list that always offers it first) and it replies in-thread a moment later, using the rest of the conversation and, if the thread is scoped to a problem, that problem's own text as context.

It won't always reply: a trivial reply to one of its own messages or a hostile/rude message gets silently ignored rather than answered.

You do not have any limits on tagging Gemini, and you can use it the way you want, but it will refuse to do anything unrelated to physics.

GeminiGlobal(ed.)Aug 9, 3:42 PM
Hi! I’m Gemini. I’m here to help you with physics — tag me with @gemini anywhere and I’ll be there faster than you can say “moment of inertia.”
Preview of Gemini replies in the forum.

subsections.title: Moderation & flags
subsections.html:
Every message, including Gemini's own replies, is automatically screened before it ever appears, so most disallowed content never gets posted in the first place.

If something slips through, any message can be flagged after the fact. A flag sends that message (with a bit of surrounding thread context) for automatic review, which either clears it or removes it. There's no manual queue to wait on. Repeated removals against the same person add up: enough of them in a short window leads to a temporary posting ban, shown as a countdown banner right in the composer, with the ban length increasing if it keeps happening.

BornGlobal(ed.)Aug 9, 3:41 PM
Maxwell would tell you it’s over for you, give up!
BornGlobal(ed.)Aug 9, 3:41 PM
Maxwell would tell you it’s over for you, give up!
BornGlobal(ed.)Aug 9, 3:41 PM
This message was removed by auto-moderation after being flagged. Reason: harassment.
MaxwellGlobal(ed.)Aug 9, 3:41 PM
Maybe my demon, but not me! Keep going!
Four snapshots of how flagging plays out. The first three are the same message by Born as it moves through moderation: Gray flag, not yet flagged, the default idle state every message starts in. Yellow flag, someone flagged it and it is being auto-reviewed. Red flag, review finished and the message was removed, the body is replaced by a removal notice the same way a real deletion renders. The last one, by Maxwell, shows a different outcome: Green flag, the message was flagged, but the review found no violation, so it stays up and the flag just marks it as reviewed.

subsections.title: What gets tracked
subsections.html:
Every Random 6 attempt you check gets logged: the quiz set, single/cumulative mode, your score, how long it took, and the value and unit you typed for each individual problem. That per-problem detail is what lets you reopen an old attempt later and see exactly what you answered, not just the final score.

Solve Them All doesn’t log attempts here the way Random 6 does; its own progress is tracked separately and covered on the next page.

No identifying information is collected by the platform’s backend. The database strictly stores only a randomly generated device UUID, the nickname you choose, and a secure hash of your PIN when you claim an identity. Absolutely no data regarding your email address or browser details is saved to the database. Everything is kept purely locally on your device until you claim a nickname, at which point it starts syncing under that identity instead.

Separately, the hosting provider automatically retains standard network operational data for up to 30 days. This includes your IP address, user-agent information, specific request details, and server performance metrics. You can read the full details of how this data is handled via Netlify’s GDPR and CCPA statement.

All your data is stored securely using Supabase, with the primary database node located in Tokyo, Japan. As a data processor, Supabase acts under strict developer instructions to safeguard this user content, maintaining infrastructure logs strictly for performance management, platform optimization, and security. You can review how they protect data and infrastructure by reading the Supabase Privacy Policy, their Terms of Service, and their overview on Logs & Analytics.

Currently, the platform does not feature an automated account deletion procedure. However, if you wish to delete your account, I’ll probably have to code one up for you.

subsections.title: Cross-device sync
subsections.html:
Sync piggybacks on the same claimed nickname + PIN identity the forum uses, rather than a separate account system. Claiming a nickname links your device’s random ID to that identity server-side; any other device that claims (or logs back into) the same nickname gets linked to it too, and from then on both devices read and write the same data.

Two things sync this way:

Random 6 attempts are pushed up and the full list is pulled back down each time you sync, so a new attempt from any linked device shows up in your log everywhere else. Re-uploading the same attempt twice (say, after a flaky connection) is automatically recognized and skipped rather than creating a duplicate. Deleting an attempt removes it from every device the next time each one syncs.

Solve Them All progress syncs per quiz set, merging rather than overwriting: if you’ve solved further on your phone than your laptop had recorded, syncing brings the laptop up to date without undoing anything either device had already gotten right.

Not everything syncs. Appearance settings like your color theme and filter preferences stay local to each device, and nothing at all leaves your device until you claim a nickname.

subsections.title: Exporting your data
subsections.html:
The Export stats button, in the Attempt log header, saves your full attempt history as a file. It always covers everything you've ever logged, regardless of whatever quiz or mode filters are currently narrowing the table on screen.

Four formats are offered, all built from the same summary: Quiz, Mode, Date & Time, Duration, and Score for every attempt.

Exports don't include your saved per-problem answers, just the attempt-level summary above; open an attempt from the log itself if you want to review exactly what you typed on each problem.

subsections.title: Themes & fonts
subsections.html:
Every screen can be recolored two independent ways: pick one of six built-in color themes from the palette button, and separately flip between daylight and night mode with the sun/moon toggle. Any theme works in either mode. The choice lives only on this device — unlike quiz progress, appearance settings don’t sync across devices. Each window below shows a theme’s night half (left) and day half (right) side by side.

Default
Default — modeled on GitHub’s own dark interface, familiar to anyone who’s stared at a diff at 2am.
Nord
Nord — the well-known arctic palette popular in code editors: cool grays with a frosty blue accent.
Sakura
Sakura — cherry-blossom pink with the roundest corners of any preset, for a softer, cozier feel.
Cyber
Cyber — neon cyberpunk glow, near-zero corner rounding, and Space Grotesk type for a sharper edge.
Forest
Forest — earthy woodland greens and browns, calm and grounded.
Solar
Solar — built on the classic Solarized color scheme, warm and desaturated with generous curves.
Custom
Custom — whatever you’ve set up in the custom theme builder, previewed live from your saved settings. Click to switch to it.

Fonts

IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono are the default UI pairing everywhere outside a themed override. Space Grotesk/Space Mono take over under Cyber, Quicksand under Sakura, and Bangers is reserved for the landing screen’s splash text. Problem statements and every rendered equation use STIX Two Text, a serif built for math typesetting, so formulas read like they belong in an actual physics textbook instead of a UI font stretched to do double duty.

Custom theme

The custom builder skips picking every variable by hand: set a background, text, and two accent colors separately for night and day, plus a corner-roundness slider and one of four font pairings (Plex, Grotesk, Quicksand, or all-mono). Surface panels, borders, and muted text are auto-derived by blending your background toward your text color, with a live preview before you save.

subsections.title: About the project
subsections.html:
This project started small, in June 2026, when I took PHYS 162 in the summer term. To be precise, it wasn’t even a webpage yet: I just shared a single HTML file with my peers in the group. There were no other modes besides a random set of 6 problems, no forum, no themes, no stats, no changelog, not even unit parsing (initially you just entered the number in SI with no units). Just a quick way to practice PHYS 162 without digging through a PDF.

Aoi-Kuro/impulseView on GitHub ↗
Loading live stats…

Then it grew step by step, as you can see in the changelog: solve-them-all mode, a daylight switcher, $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ support, and more. One of the biggest flexes of this project is that I manually redrew every figure from the problem sets as dynamic illustrations, using Adobe Illustrator and some HTML magic. A lot of smaller UI work went uncovered along the way too: for instance, every time you open Solve Them All mode, all the $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ expressions are pre-rendered and cached locally, so the next time you open the quiz you don’t have to wait for it.

I also tried to make the site feel like more than a dead screen that just tells you your score. Splashes, a few easter eggs, and a forum went in to make it feel alive.

Splashes from the main screen. Give it a tap!

The forum, actually, was a suggestion from a friend of mine who wasn’t even using the site, not something I’d originally planned. It grew from a simple read-only feed into a full system with nicknames, PINs, $\mathrm{La\TeX}$ support, moderation, mentions, and replies. This manual you’re reading right now is the newest addition, built the same way: as a request, then built out properly rather than left as an afterthought.

Aside from learning PHYS 162, I hoped this could show what enthusiasm alone can do. I didn’t know a thing about web development, database design, or anything else you see here when I started: I only had the desire to do it. And here we are.

Whether you think you can, or you think you can’t — you’re right.

Henry Ford

subsections.title: Feedback & Contact
subsections.html:
Found a bug, a typo, or a wrong answer key on one of the problems? Message me on Telegram, @Aoi_Kuro. Small fixes like a mistake in a problem's answer key, a spelling error, or a broken formula usually go out fast; I will likely do it on the spot, so most of these get sorted the same day.

Prefer GitHub?Open an issue ↗
Loading live stats…

Bigger feature requests are welcome too: send them the same way. Nothing about this site is fixed in stone; the forum itself started as exactly this kind of suggestion. I can't promise a timeline on anything larger, since it depends on free time between coursework, but I do keep a list and go through it when I get a proper break. If enough people ask for the same thing, that moves it up.

So: small stuff gets fixed fast, big stuff gets considered and maybe built for whoever's using this site next.
